extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics / introductory mathematical logic
extracted.subtask_description: Translate English mathematical or everyday statements into predicate logic with quantifiers, and manipulate/interpret formulas (negation, equivalence, order of quantifiers, bounded quantifiers, etc.). Includes worked examples and exercises for understanding truth and equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stepwise translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate English into symbols in several steps, translating only a little bit at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the sentence into manageable pieces and convert each piece into symbolic form before combining. Example: (i) plain English paraphrase, (ii) add quantifiers/structure, (iii) replace English phrases by predicate symbols to obtain the final formula (see the quarantined-friend example: steps (i)–(iii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual interpretation of ambiguous words (e.g., 'anyone')
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'anyone' can mean different things in different contexts (everyone vs someone); determine the intended meaning from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the sentence structure: e.g., in one example 'anyone' meant everyone (∀), in another it meant someone (∃). Show intermediate paraphrases to decide which quantifier fits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read quantifiers one at a time (outer-to-inner)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement contains more than one quantifier, think about the quantifiers one at a time in order (usually outermost first).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret ∀x∃y(...) by first fixing x and then asking what the inner ∃y(...) means for that x. This helps determine truth by testing particular values (illustrated with ∀x∃y(x+y=5)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of quantifiers matters (∀ vs ∃)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing the order of different types of quantifiers can change the meaning of a formula (e.g., ∀x∃y vs ∃y∀x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples to see the difference: ∀x∃y(x+y=5) is true over R (y depends on x), whereas ∃y∀x(x+y=5) is false (single y cannot satisfy all x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Same-type quantifiers commute
rubrics_metrics.description: If the quantifiers are the same type (both ∀ or both ∃), their order can be switched without affecting meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ∀x∀y and ∀y∀x both mean 'for all x and y'; ∃x∃y and ∃y∃x both mean 'there exist x and y such that...'. Example: ∃x∃y(T(y,x) ∧ P(y,x)) ≡ ∃y∃x(...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce distinctness explicitly when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a statement requires different objects (e.g., 'at least two different people'), include inequality constraints like y ≠ z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume different quantified variables denote different objects. Example: 'Everyone likes at least two people' requires ∃y∃z(L(x,y) ∧ L(x,z) ∧ y ≠ z). For 'bigamist' add y ≠ z when using ∃y∃z(M(x,y) ∧ M(x,z)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantiﬁer negation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation interacts with quantifiers via the laws ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x) and ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to move negation past quantifiers and to reexpress negative statements as equivalent positive ones. Examples: ¬∃x P(x) ↔ ∀x¬P(x); ¬∀x P(x) ↔ ∃x¬P(x). Combined with DeMorgan and conditional laws to simplify negations (see exercises and worked negations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negating bounded quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounded quantifiers obey the same negation laws: ¬∀x∈A P(x) ≡ ∃x∈A ¬P(x) and ¬∃x∈A P(x) ≡ ∀x∈A ¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive these by expanding bounded quantifiers to unbounded forms (∀x∈A P(x) ≡ ∀x(x∈A → P(x))) and then applying the usual quantifier negation and propositional equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bounded quantifier notation to indicate universe or restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Write ∀x∈U P(x) or ∃x∈U P(x) to make explicit which universe or subset is in play; these are abbreviations for implication/and-clauses with unbounded quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ∀x∈R+ ∃y∈R− (y^2 = x) expands to ∀x(x∈R+ → ∃y(y∈R− ∧ y^2 = x)). Use this to avoid confusion about domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacuous truth for universals over empty sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = ∅ then ∃x∈A P(x) is false for any P, while ∀x∈A P(x) is true (vacuously true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify using quantifier negation: ∀x∈A P(x) ≡ ¬∃x∈A ¬P(x); with A empty the existential is false, so the universal is true. Apply to facts like ∅ ⊆ B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal quantifier distributes over conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: ∀x (E(x) ∧ T(x)) is equivalent to (∀x E(x)) ∧ (∀x T(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret as 'everyone is bright-eyed and everyone is bushy-tailed' ≡ 'everyone is bright-eyed, and everyone is bushy-tailed.' Use this when splitting universal statements into component parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential quantifier does not distribute over conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: ∃x (E(x) ∧ T(x)) is not equivalent to (∃x E(x)) ∧ (∃x T(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The left asserts one object satisfying both properties; the right only asserts possibly two (different) objects, one with E and one with T. Use truth-set intuition: left says A∩B ≠ ∅, right says A ≠ ∅ and B ≠ ∅.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate set-theoretic statements to quantified logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Set relations like A ⊆ B, A = B, A ar{}⊆ etc. have quantified equivalents (e.g., A ⊆ B ≡ ∀x(x∈A → x∈B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negations and manipulations follow from quantifier laws: e.g., ¬(A⊆B) ≡ ∃x(x∈A ∧ x∉B). Use these translations to prove equivalences like A = B ↔ (A⊆B ∧ B⊆A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use uniqueness quantifier expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Express 'there is exactly one x such that P(x)' using ∃!x P(x) as abbreviation for ∃x(P(x) ∧ ¬∃y(P(y) ∧ y ≠ x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing 'exactly one' or 'unique', either use ∃! notation or expand to the conjunction of existence and uniqueness as above (illustrated by 'John likes exactly one person').

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing truth of quantified formulas with examples
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine truth, try particular values for outer quantifiers and examine inner quantified statements; use concrete instances and algebraic solving when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: plug x=2,7 into ∃y(x+y=5) to see the inner existential holds for each x; show no fixed y makes ∀x(x+y=5) true. For natural numbers, reason about bounds (e.g., ∃y∀x(x<y) false).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed-family and elementhood translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate notation {x_i | i∈I} to quantified formulas: x∈{x_i | i∈I} ≡ ∃i∈I (x = x_i); statements about such families can be written with quantifiers over the index set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can express subset or membership claims either as ∀i∈I (x_i ∈ A) or as ∀x(∃i∈I (x=x_i) → x∈A). Use whichever is clearer for the context (see examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply propositional equivalences when manipulating quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine quantifier laws with propositional equivalences (De Morgan, conditional laws, double negation) to reexpress and simplify formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text show sequences of equivalences: ¬∀x∃y(...) → ∃x¬∃y(...) → ∃x∀y¬(...) → ∃x∀y(...). Use these systematic steps to transform negations and derive equivalent positive statements.
